tiktokData.title: The Tax Bracket Myth Most Canadians Believe

info.text:
A higher tax bracket never taxes your whole income. 🇨🇦

Only the slice above the line pays the higher rate. With $60K of taxable income, just $1,477 is taxed at 20.5% federally; the rest stays at 14% (2026). Real example, Manitoba: a $2,000 raise → you keep $1,292.

The one exception: benefits like the Canada Child Benefit shrink as family income rises. On benefits? Run the numbers with a pro.

Send this to the coworker who thinks a raise can cost them money.

One real exception: income-tested benefits like the Canada Child Benefit shrink as family income rises (reduction starts above $38,237 of adjusted family net income for July 2026 – June 2027). On benefits? Run your numbers with a professional.

info.text:
Your parents aren't a tax deduction. But they CAN count for 3 credits, if one condition is met. 🇨🇦

Money you send home isn't deductible in Canada: deductible support is for a spouse or ex-partner (or your child's other parent) under a court order or written agreement. A parent can count for the Canada caregiver amount, medical expenses or the eligible dependant amount, but the residency and living-with-you rules decide it.

Save this before tax season, and send it to anyone who supports family abroad.

#canadiantaxes #personalfinancecanada #newcomerstocanada #immigrantsincanada #cra #canadatax
info.firstCommentText: Who here supports parents back home? 🙋 Which country, and did they ever live with you in Canada?

info.text:
Sending money to your parents back home? In most cases it's not tax-deductible in Canada. Here's what CRA actually allows.

Deductible support payments are spousal support (a current or former partner, or your child's other parent, under a court order or written agreement). Parents aren't on that list. Three tax credits CAN include a parent: the Canada caregiver amount (line 30450), medical expenses (line 33199) and the eligible dependant amount (line 30400). The catch: for a parent, the first two require them to be resident in Canada at some point in the year, and the third requires them to live with you.

Bringing parents to Canada? Residency depends on the facts. Get professional advice and keep proof of support.

Sources: CRA, support payments; lines 30400, 30450, 33199 (canada.ca). $500/month is an example. General information, not tax advice.

tiktokData.title: What Happens to Your RRSP at 71? (Don't Miss Dec 31)

info.text:
Turning 71 this year? Your RRSP has a December 31 deadline. 🇨🇦

By the end of the year you turn 71, an RRSP must be cashed out, used to buy an annuity, or transferred to a RRIF. Cash out = it's all income that year (30% withheld on a lump sum over $15,000, outside Québec). Annuity or RRIF = no tax withheld on the direct transfer; you're taxed as payments come in. RRIF minimum at 72: 5.40%.

Save this and share it with someone turning 71.

Sources: CRA (canada.ca). $300,000 is an example. General info, not advice.

#rrsp #rrif #retirementplanning #canadiantaxes #personalfinancecanada #canadatax
info.firstCommentText: Who in your family turns 71 this year? 🙋 Have they picked cash, annuity or RRIF yet?

info.text:
Turning 71 this year? Your RRSP has to be closed by December 31: cash it out, buy an annuity, or transfer it to a RRIF.

Cash out: the whole amount is income that year, and on a lump sum over $15,000 the issuer withholds 30% (outside Québec). On $300,000 that's $90,000 withheld up front, and it isn't even the final tax. Annuity or RRIF: no tax is withheld on the direct transfer; you're taxed as the payments come in. RRIF withdrawals start the year after; at 72 the minimum is 5.40% of the value (on $300,000: $16,200), with no tax withheld on the minimum, but it's still income.

The real danger is doing nothing: if the plan no longer qualifies as an RRSP, CRA treats you as having received the full value as income.

Choosing or mixing options depends on your situation. Talk to your issuer and a tax professional.

Sources: CRA (canada.ca): RRSP options when you turn 71, Tax rates on withdrawals, Minimum amount from a RRIF, T4040. $300,000 is an example. General information, not tax advice.

#RRSP #RRIF #CanadaTax

Over $95K in retirement? 🇨🇦 Here's how the OAS clawback really works, and 3 legal ways to keep more.

#oas #retirementcanada #canadiantaxes #personalfinancecanada #seniorscanada
info.firstCommentText: Which lever would help your family most: splitting, TFSA or delaying OAS? (General info, not advice.)

tiktokData.title: OAS Clawback 2026: The $95,323 Line (and 3 Legal Ways to Keep More)

info.text:
The OAS clawback isn't a penalty on all your OAS. It's 15¢ per $1 above a line. 🇨🇦

For 2026 income the line is $95,323. Example: $110,000 net income → $14,677 over → $2,201.55 recovered from OAS paid July 2027 – June 2028.

3 legal levers: pension income splitting at 65+ (up to 50% of eligible pension income), TFSA withdrawals (not income), and delaying OAS (+0.6% a month, up to 36% at 70).

Save this, and share it with a parent near the line.

Sources: Service Canada / CRA (canada.ca). $110,000 is an example. General info, not advice.

#oas #oldagesecurity #retirementplanning #canadiantaxes #personalfinancecanada #canadatax
info.firstCommentText: Is anyone in your family near $95K of retirement income? 🙋 Which lever surprised you most?

info.text:
Retired with income over $95,323? Part of your Old Age Security goes back. Here's exactly how much, and three legal levers.

The OAS recovery tax: for 2026 income, you repay 15% of your net world income above $95,323. Example: net income of $110,000 is $14,677 over the line, so $2,201.55 is recovered, withheld from your OAS payments from July 2027 to June 2028.

Three legal levers:
1) Pension income splitting: at 65+, up to 50% of eligible pension income (including RRIF and annuity payments) can be allocated to your spouse (joint election, Form T1032).
2) TFSA withdrawals aren't income, so they don't affect OAS.
3) Delaying OAS: +0.6% for each month after 65, up to +36% at 70 (you can't get GIS while you delay).

Which lever fits depends on your whole picture. Talk to a tax professional.

Sources: Service Canada, OAS pension recovery tax; CRA, Pension income splitting; What is a TFSA; OAS: when to start (canada.ca). $110,000 is an example. General information, not tax advice.

CPP at 60, 65 or 70? 🇨🇦 −36% or +42%, for life. Here's the real math.

#cpp #retirementcanada #canadiantaxes #personalfinancecanada #retirementplanning
info.firstCommentText: 60, 65 or 70: which one are you leaning toward, and why? (General info, not advice.)

tiktokData.title: CPP at 60, 65 or 70? The Real Math

info.text:
Same pension, three very different cheques. 🇨🇦

CPP at 60: −0.6% for each month before 65, up to −36%, for life. CPP at 70: +0.7% for each month after 65, up to +42%. Example: $1,000 at 65 = $640 at 60, $1,420 at 70.

Simplified break-even for waiting from 65 to 70: about age 82, and about half of today's retirees reach 90 (Retirement Hub). Health changes the answer.

Save this, and share it with someone turning 60.

Sources: Service Canada (canada.ca). $1,000 is an example. General info, not advice.

#cpp #canadapensionplan #retirementplanning #canadiantaxes #personalfinancecanada #canadatax
info.firstCommentText: 60, 65 or 70? 🙋 Which would you choose for your own situation?

info.text:
Take CPP at 60, or wait until 70? The difference is permanent.

Start before 65 and your CPP retirement pension is reduced by 0.6% for each month, up to 36% at 60. Wait past 65 and it grows 0.7% a month, up to 42% at 70. Example: if your pension would be $1,000 a month at 65, it's $640 at 60 and $1,420 at 70, more than double from 60 to 70.

Simplified break-even (ignoring inflation, tax and returns): waiting from 65 to 70 pays off if you live past about 82. The federal Retirement Hub notes about half of today's retirees will reach 90. Health matters: with serious health concerns, earlier may make sense; in good health, later may pay more.

It's a lifetime decision. Run your own numbers (My Service Canada Account shows your estimate) and get advice.

Sources: Service Canada, CPP: When to start your pension; Retirement Hub (canada.ca). $1,000 is an example. General information, not financial advice.

#CPP #RetirementCanada #CanadaTax

info.text:

info.firstCommentText: Expect your tax rate to be higher or lower later? That's your answer. (General info, not advice.)

tiktokData.title: RRSP or TFSA? One Question Decides It

info.text:
RRSP or TFSA? One question decides it. 🇨🇦

RRSP: deducted now, taxed when it comes out. TFSA: taxed now, tax-free when it comes out (and the room comes back next year).
Same tax rate in and out → the same result ($1,000 that doubles → $1,400 either way, at 30%). Lower rate later → RRSP ahead. Higher later → TFSA ahead.

2026 limits: TFSA $7,000 · RRSP 18% of last year's earned income, up to $33,810.

Save this for contribution season.

Source: CRA (canada.ca). Illustration only, not investment advice.

#rrsp #tfsa #personalfinancecanada #canadiantaxes #savingmoney #canadatax
info.firstCommentText: RRSP team or TFSA team? 🙋 And why?

info.text:
RRSP or TFSA? It isn't about which one is "better". It's your tax rate now versus later.

RRSP: contributions are deductible, so you save tax today, but withdrawals are taxed as income.
TFSA: no deduction going in, but growth and withdrawals are tax-free, and the amount you withdraw comes back as contribution room on January 1 of the next year.

Illustration: $1,000 of income that doubles, at the same 30% rate going in and coming out, leaves $1,400 in either account. A lower rate later (20%) favours the RRSP ($1,600); a higher rate later (40%) favours the TFSA ($1,400 vs $1,200).

2026 limits: TFSA $7,000 (plus unused room); RRSP 18% of last year's earned income, up to $33,810. Check your own room in CRA My Account.

Sources: CRA (canada.ca). The example is an illustration. Mechanics only, not investment advice.

info.text:
65 or older on a low income? The Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) is a monthly, tax-free payment on top of OAS, and the government's own estimate says about 240,000 eligible seniors didn't receive it in 2015.

tiktokData.title: Can You Write It Off? CRA's First Question

info.text:
Can you write it off? CRA's first question: did you spend it to earn income? 🇨🇦

✓ Reasonable cost to earn business income → deductible. Personal → not.
✓ Mixed use → the business part only ($1,200 phone × 60% = $720, example).
✓ Lasts for years → claimed over time (CCA).
✓ Meals & entertainment → generally 50%.
✓ Employees → only if your contract requires it (T2200).
✓ Keep records → generally 6 years.

Save this for tax season.

Source: CRA (canada.ca). General info, not advice.

#smallbusinesscanada #selfemployedcanada #canadiantaxes #taxtips #entrepreneurcanada #canadatax
info.firstCommentText: Self-employed or salaried? 🙋 Which rule surprised you?

info.text:
Can you write it off? Before anything else, CRA asks: did you spend it to earn income?

The general rule (CRA Guide T4002): a reasonable current expense you incur to earn business income is deductible; personal costs are not. Mixed use? Claim only the business part (example: a $1,200 phone bill used 60% for the business = $720).
Something that lasts for years, like a laptop or a car, isn't deducted all at once; it's claimed over time through capital cost allowance (CCA).
Business meals and entertainment: generally only 50%.
On a salary? You can deduct employment expenses only if your contract requires you to pay them (your employer signs Form T2200).
And keep the proof: records generally for six years.

Sources: CRA (canada.ca): T4002, line 8523, T4044, Business records. The phone example is an illustration. General information, not advice.

info.text:
Throwing out old receipts? CRA can ask for them years later.

Generally, keep your records for six years; for business records, six years from the end of the tax year they relate to. Example: business receipts for 2026 → keep until at least the end of 2032.
Exceptions: filed late? The six years start when you file. Disputing an assessment (objection or appeal)? Keep everything until it's resolved.
Scans and digital files count, as long as they're complete and readable. Want to destroy records sooner? You need CRA's permission first (Form T137).

Freelancing in Canada and getting close to $30,000? The GST/HST threshold isn't counted per calendar year. It's any four consecutive calendar quarters.

Example: $5,000 + $8,000 + $9,000 + $9,500 over four quarters = $31,500, over the line. You stop being a small supplier at the end of the month after that quarter, then you have 29 days to register. Cross $30,000 in a single quarter and you charge GST/HST on the very sale that put you over.

Paying for daycare? Part of it can come off your taxable income, but usually only one parent can claim it.

What can count: daycare centres, nursery schools, caregivers like babysitters or nannies, and day camps. Yearly limit per child: $8,000 under age 7, $5,000 from 7 to 16 ($11,000 if the child is eligible for the disability tax credit).

Generally, the parent with the lower net income claims it, and the claim is capped at two-thirds of that parent's earned income. Example: parents earning $90,000 and $30,000, $9,000 of daycare for a 3-year-old → the $30,000 parent claims $8,000.

The higher earner claims only in specific cases (e.g. the other parent was in school or in hospital), with weekly limits on Form T778. Keep every receipt; for a babysitter, their SIN must be on it. And because it lowers net income, it can help your Canada Child Benefit too.

info.text:
How does a small corporation in Manitoba pay just 9% tax on its profit? The small business deduction.

On the first $500,000 of active business income, a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) pays 9% federal tax, and Manitoba adds 0%. Above that, the general rate applies: 27% combined (15% federal + 12% Manitoba).

Example: $120,000 of profit → about $10,800 of corporate tax instead of $32,400.

Two traps: passive investment income over $50,000 inside the company shrinks the $500,000 limit ($5 for every $1, gone at $150,000), and an incorporated employee (a personal services business) doesn't get the deduction at all. Associated companies share one limit.

And it's a deferral, not a gift: when you pay yourself dividends, you pay personal tax on them.

Losses offset gains only (back 3 years, forward indefinitely). Rebuy within 30 days → the loss is denied. In a TFSA: generally not taxed.

info.text:
Sold a stock for a profit? In Canada you're not taxed on all of it: only half.

Your capital gain = selling price − your cost (the adjusted cost base) − selling costs. Example: bought shares for $10,000, sold for $16,000, $50 in fees → a $5,950 gain. Only half, $2,975, is added to your income and taxed at your regular rate.

The proposed increase of the inclusion rate to two-thirds was cancelled: it's still one-half.

Capital losses only offset capital gains; unused net capital losses can be carried back 3 years or forward indefinitely. One trap: sell at a loss and buy the same shares back within 30 days (before or after), and the loss is denied (superficial loss). Inside a TFSA, gains are generally not taxed.

Track your cost base: every sale goes on your return (Schedule 3).

Sources: CRA guide T4037; Department of Finance (canada.ca). The share sale is an example. General information, not advice.
